questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: From import substitution to export orientation
questions.learningObjective: Explain what import substitution meant and why it was later abandoned
questions.stem: Sheet 77 asks the cartographer to note what import substitution meant and why later governments turned away from it.

options.text: It meant building domestic factories to replace imports, with tariffs and overvalued rates protecting them
options.misconception: describes import substitution as the abandoned approach

options.text: It was an early strategy of making goods at home that were previously imported, and it later stalled
It was a rule that let a country buy anything it liked from abroad at a fixed price
options.misconception: invents a free-trade rule under the label

options.text: It was the post-war agreement that fixed exchange rates for the leading trading nations
options.misconception: confuses the term with the fixed rate agreement

questions.explanation: Import substitution meant replacing imported goods with domestic production, usually shielded by tariffs and an overvalued currency. Describing it as a free-trade rule misstates the term.
questions.hint: Ask what was made at home instead of bought.

questions.topic: Reading the export composition of a growing region
questions.learningObjective: Read export composition to judge how broad a region's export base is
questions.stem: Legend entry 12 shows a table in which textiles take 41 percent of a region's export earnings, machinery 28 percent, food 19 percent and other goods 12 percent, and asks how the legend should read.

options.text: The region is fully diversified, because four different product groups are present
options.misconception: counts product groups as diversification

options.text: The region has a narrow base, because textiles alone take more than a third of earnings
options.misconception: reads a moderate share as a narrow base

options.text: The region has a narrow base, because no single product reaches half of all earnings
options.misconception: uses a threshold of half to declare breadth

options.text: The region has a moderately broad base, with one leading line and three others of real size

questions.explanation: A leading line of 41 percent alongside three lines of real size describes a base broader than a single export but not fully spread. Calling it narrow misreads the table.
questions.hint: Compare the largest line with the rest.

questions.topic: Reading a default on a foreign currency loan
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a currency move caused a default on foreign currency debt
questions.stem: Projection note 301 says the sheet explains a default as a failure of effort and asks the cartographer to correct it.

options.text: The borrower could not earn the loan's currency to meet it, so the debt grew faster than its income
The borrower failed to try hard enough, and better administration would have avoided the default
options.misconception: blames effort rather than the currency mismatch

options.text: The lender was unwise to lend, and any default shows a failure of credit judgement
options.misconception: makes the default a symptom of lender error

options.text: The default was unavoidable, because the borrower's government had spent all the money
options.misconception: reduces the default to the government's spending

questions.explanation: A default on foreign currency debt often arises because the borrower earns in one currency and owes in another, so the burden rises without any change in effort.
questions.hint: Ask what currency the borrower earns in.

questions.topic: What the first defaults revealed about lending
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the first defaults revealed about lending practice

stimulus.body: We note that the borrowers who defaulted were not those who borrowed for ordinary trade, but those who borrowed in a currency they did not earn and then saw it fall. We propose that the committee consider the currency of the borrower's export earnings before the currency of the loan.

questions.stem: Grid note 19 attaches a lending committee minute to the sheet and asks what it shows.

options.text: The minute shows the committee blaming the borrowers for their own mistakes in borrowing
options.misconception: reads the minute as a blame exercise

options.text: The minute shows the committee proposing to lend less to countries with weak exports
options.misconception: misreads the proposal as a rule about export volume

options.text: The minute shows the committee learning to price the currency mismatch into its decisions
The minute shows the committee deciding to stop lending to smaller countries
options.misconception: invents a policy on borrower size

questions.explanation: The minute links the defaults to the currency of the loan rather than the borrower's character, and proposes a change in how credit is assessed.
questions.hint: Ask what the committee proposed to check.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Financing aid without taxing what it builds
questions.learningObjective: Explain why aid-financed works could not be taxed at the point of use
questions.stem: Scale caption 8 asks for a written account of why money spent on a new port could not easily be raised by tax.

answer.exemplar: The port was meant to earn foreign currency from handling other people's trade, and the customs duties collected at it were the obvious source for a tax on its use. But a tax collected on the port's traffic would be paid by the shipping lines and merchants who chose to call there, and if it was high enough to matter they would simply go elsewhere. Raising the money from domestic income instead meant asking the country's own taxpayers, who had no interest in a harbour serving foreign trade, to pay for it.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains why a tax on the activity itself would drive the activity away, and why domestic taxpayers then bore the cost. Naming the burden alone misses it.
questions.hint: Explain what a tax on the traffic would do.

options.text: The bargain was designed to be free of rules, so that no party could complain of an obligation
options.misconception: invents an absence of rules as the design goal

options.text: The bargain was designed to favour the largest trading party, whose consent mattered most
options.misconception: makes the design a favour to the largest party

options.text: The bargain was designed to avoid rules on the goods traded, and covered only the paperwork
options.misconception: claims the new rules were narrower than the old

options.text: The bargain was designed to give smaller states a share, so that the old imbalance could not block it

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the earlier imbalance to the requirement that the new bargain give smaller states a share. A favour to the largest party misses the logic.
questions.hint: Show what the earlier rules left out.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why fixed exchange rates returned after the 1930s
questions.stem: Fold annotation 6 asks the cartographer to note why fixed exchange rates returned after the collapse of the 1930s.

options.text: Because fixed rates gave governments the certainty they needed to plan, trade and invest
Because governments had given up any wish to influence their exchange rates
options.misconception: claims states had abandoned control of the rate

options.text: Because gold was so plentiful that no one needed a fixed rate to hold it steady
options.misconception: invents an abundance of gold as the reason

options.text: Because the world had decided that floating rates always failed in every case
options.misconception: generalises from past failure to a universal rule

questions.explanation: Fixed rates returned because governments wanted the certainty a stable rate gave them for trade, budgets and investment. Saying gold was plentiful misstates the reason.

questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Read reserve and holdings data to judge the strain on a metal peg
questions.stem: Atlas entry 204 shows a table in which one country's holdings of the reserve currency exceed its own gold stock by more than half, and asks what the sheet should read.

options.text: The country is in a strong position, because its holdings of the reserve currency are large
options.misconception: reads a large holding as strength, ignoring the gold

options.text: The country must soon devalue, because holdings always force a devaluation
options.misconception: claims holdings always force a devaluation

options.text: The gap between holdings and gold is a claim that cannot all be met, which strains the peg
The country has a surplus of gold, because holdings of the reserve currency are counted as gold
options.misconception: treats foreign currency holdings as metal

questions.explanation: When holdings of the reserve currency exceed the gold behind them, the promise of conversion is larger than the asset backing it. Reading the holdings as strength misreads the table.
questions.hint: Compare the two lines before drawing a conclusion.

questions.topic: From import substitution to export orientation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why import substitution stalled in the countries that adopted it
questions.stem: Sheet 84 says the sheet treats import substitution as a policy that failed everywhere and asks for the corrected account.

options.text: It failed everywhere, because protection always ends more expensive than imports
options.misconception: claims protection always costs more than imports

options.text: It worked at first in several countries and then stalled as costs and currency rose
It never worked, because the factories it created could not survive any tariff at all
options.misconception: denies that protected factories ever survived

options.text: It failed only where it was tried, and it was never tried in the poorer countries
options.misconception: invents a restriction on where it was tried

questions.explanation: The record shows an initial success in some countries followed by stalling as costs rose and the currency overvalued. Saying it failed everywhere distorts the evidence.
questions.hint: Look at the sequence, success first then stall.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the export composition of a growing region
questions.learningObjective: Draw a conclusion about export composition from a customs report

stimulus.body: Machinery exports rose by two thirds in three years and now account for more than a quarter of all earnings. Textile exports have fallen in every one of those years, and the number of firms still working in textiles is half what it was. The region now takes more machinery from abroad than it sends out of the country.

questions.stem: Legend entry 21 attaches a customs report to the sheet and asks what it shows about the region's export composition.

options.text: The report shows the region replacing an old export line with a new and more varied one
options.misconception: describes the change as simple replacement of one line

options.text: The report shows the region becoming dependent on a single new export line
options.misconception: reads one growing line as the whole structure

options.text: The report shows the region importing more machinery than it exports, so the trade is in deficit
options.misconception: treats a manufacturing position as a trade deficit

options.text: The report shows the composition of exports changing as new lines grow and old ones shrink

questions.explanation: The report shows one line expanding, another contracting and the region's manufacturing position shifting, which is a change of composition. Reading it as replacement misstates it.
questions.hint: Look at what happened to the older line.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a default on a foreign currency loan
questions.learningObjective: Trace how a currency move turned a workable loan into a default
questions.stem: Projection note 318 asks for a written explanation of how a currency move turned a workable loan into a default.

answer.exemplar: The loan was written down in a currency the borrower did not earn, and the budget assumed the rate would stay where it was. When the borrower's own currency weakened against the loan currency, the same interest and the same principal demanded more of the local currency than before, even though nothing about the project behind the loan had changed. The debt service rose as a share of export earnings while those earnings were also falling, and the two movements together exhausted the country's reserves.

questions.explanation: A good answer traces the currency move into a larger local-currency bill and then into the exhaustion of reserves. Blaming mismanagement without the currency step misses it.
questions.hint: Trace the currency move into the bill and the reserves.

options.text: The defaults produced no change, since the rules had been written for a world that had vanished
options.misconception: claims the rules were left untouched and reason why

options.text: The defaults were forgiven, so the lending rules could be written with no risk in mind
options.misconception: invents forgiveness as the route to a new rule

options.text: The defaults exposed what lending agreements had failed to specify, and the new rules filled the gap
The defaults preceded the rules, so the new lending framework was built to prevent them
options.misconception: reverses the order of defaults and rules

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect what the defaults exposed about incomplete agreements to the specifications the later rules added. Claiming no change breaks the link.
questions.hint: Show what was missing and what was added.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Financing aid without taxing what it builds
questions.learningObjective: Identify the measure that lets a financed port avoid being taxed out of use
questions.stem: Scale caption 17 asks which measure the sheet should pair with a financed port so that the port is not taxed out of existence.

options.text: A levy on the foreign shipping that uses the port, collected as part of the foreign currency earnings
options.misconception: puts the levy on the users instead of the domestic taxpayer

options.text: A charge on the domestic income of the country, so the cost falls on taxpayers rather than the traffic
A higher customs duty on imports, on the argument that the port made them dearer
options.misconception: raises the cost of the very trade the port serves

options.text: A prohibition on foreign shipping, so that only domestic vessels could use the port
options.misconception: invents a closure of the port to foreign trade

questions.explanation: Charging the country's own income keeps the cost away from the traffic the port exists to attract. Putting the levy on the shipping penalises the trade the port serves.
questions.hint: Ask who should bear the cost, not the port.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Designing a trade bargain everyone will sign
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of terms to judge what smaller states obtained
questions.stem: Compass point 63 shows a table in which one group of states received lower tariffs on a range of goods and a binding ceiling on what the larger party could change, and asks what it shows.

options.text: The larger party kept full control, since the smaller states received only a promise of goodwill
options.misconception: misses the binding ceiling the table records

options.text: The smaller states gained a preference that was entirely at the larger party's discretion
options.misconception: treats the binding ceiling as a discretionary favour

options.text: Both sides gained equally, since the terms were symmetric in every line of the table
options.misconception: claims symmetry the table does not show

options.text: The smaller states gained a guaranteed share and the larger party accepted a limit on changes

questions.explanation: A lower tariff plus a binding ceiling gives the smaller states a share that cannot be withdrawn later, which is what makes the bargain acceptable. Calling it discretion misreads the terms.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fixed rate system was meant to work in practice
questions.stem: Fold annotation 14 says the sheet treats the fixed rate system as a simple rule and asks for the corrected account.

options.text: It was an adjustable rule, since the parity could be changed when a balance of payments shifted
It was simple, because every currency was pegged to the same metal at the same weight
options.misconception: overstates the uniformity of the system

options.text: It was a rigid rule, since no parity was ever changed after the system began
options.misconception: claims the parities never moved

options.text: It was a market rule, since the rates were set by the flow of trade between the countries
options.misconception: recasts the system as a market determination

questions.explanation: The system was adjustable: a parity could be moved when a country's payments position made the old one untenable, though such moves were rare. Calling it rigid misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask what happened when a balance of payments shifted.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Explain the link between the reserve currency and the metal promise

stimulus.body: We hold foreign currency in place of metal, and we expect to be able to exchange it for metal at the rate we publish. We note that the other central banks hold more of the same currency than there is metal in the vaults of all of them together, and we do not think this arrangement can last indefinitely.

questions.stem: Atlas entry 212 attaches a reserve bank note to the sheet and asks what it shows about the peg.

options.text: The note shows the central banks holding more metal than the other holders had assumed
options.misconception: invents a metal surplus the note does not claim

options.text: The note shows a deliberate plan to convert foreign holdings into metal over time
options.misconception: reads a note about strain as a conversion programme

options.text: The note shows the central banks relying on a promise that the metal behind it cannot cover
The note shows the reserve banks deciding to abandon the exchange promise at once
options.misconception: turns a question about durability into an immediate decision

questions.explanation: The note states the exchange promise and observes that the currency outstanding exceeded the metal behind it, which strained the peg. Reading it as a metal surplus contradicts the words.
questions.hint: Compare the promise with the metal behind it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: From import substitution to export orientation
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a country that had built factories to replace imports turned to exporting
questions.stem: Sheet 91 asks for a written account of why a country that had built factories to replace imports turned to exporting instead.

answer.exemplar: The factories had been built behind high tariffs and an exchange rate set too strong, so their costs stayed above what imported goods would have cost even after the tariffs were removed. Selling abroad meant competing on price in markets where nobody knew the firm, and selling at home meant the same old protected market. Export orientation followed because the sheltered strategy had run out of room, not because anyone had decided in advance that exports were better.

questions.explanation: A good answer links the protection, the cost gap and the loss of the sheltered market to the turn towards exports. A change of mind alone misses the cost argument.
questions.hint: Explain why the sheltered market stopped sheltering.

options.misconception: claims concentration strengthens a seller's position

options.text: It made the position stronger, because several buyers for several lines leave fewer ways to be squeezed

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the spread of export lines to the number of alternative buyers, which reduces pressure on any one of them. Saying breadth weakens the position misses the link.
questions.hint: Ask how many buyers the region can turn to.

questions.stem: Projection note 335 asks which description the sheet should carry for a default on a foreign currency loan.

options.text: A mismatch between the currency of the debt and the currency the country earns in
A decision by the government to stop paying, made for reasons of domestic politics
options.misconception: recasts a currency mismatch as a political refusal

options.text: A failure of the lenders, who should have checked the currency of the borrower's earnings
options.misconception: makes the default an error of the lender

options.misconception: invents a stated intention to defer payment

questions.explanation: A foreign currency default is usually read through the mismatch between the currency owed and the currency earned. Calling it a political refusal substitutes a story.

questions.topic: What the first defaults revealed about lending
questions.learningObjective: Read recovery data to judge what changed after the first defaults
questions.stem: Grid note 33 shows a table of recovery rates on defaulted loans and asks the cartographer to read it.

options.text: Lenders learned to lend better, so the newer loans recovered much more
options.misconception: attributes the difference to lending skill alone

options.text: The table shows nothing, because recovery rates depend on each case and cannot be averaged
options.misconception: denies that an average can inform the reader

The borrowers in the later period were stronger, so their better recovery was deserved

questions.topic: Financing aid without taxing what it builds
questions.learningObjective: Explain the tension between financing a project and taxing the people who use it
questions.stem: Scale caption 26 says the sheet presents the financing question as a moral one and asks for the corrected account.

options.text: It was moral, because wealthy groups must pay more for projects that serve them
options.misconception: turns a technical question into a matter of virtue

options.text: It was technical, because the choice of payer determined whether the project paid for itself
It was political, because the government wanted to avoid the voters who used the port

questions.topic: Designing a trade bargain everyone will sign

It is prepared to accept a binding ceiling on the other party's right to alter the schedule, and it asks only that the ceiling be reviewed at a fixed date by both parties together.

options.misconception: turns a condition into a refusal

options.text: The memorandum shows the smaller side seeking a limit on change and a joint review

questions.explanation: The memorandum sets out a condition, a ceiling on unilateral revision, and a joint review at a fixed date, which is a position about certainty. Calling it a refusal misreads it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain the mechanism by which a fixed rate system was meant to hold
questions.stem: Fold annotation 22 asks for a written account of how a fixed rate system was supposed to work in practice.

answer.exemplar: Each government set the value of its currency against the metal and then stood ready to buy or sell foreign currency at that fixed price, so that the rate could not drift. For the rate to hold, the country's payments position had to stay roughly in balance, and the reserves of metal and foreign currency were held for the days when it did not. The central reserve banks also adjusted the values of their own currencies together when they judged the whole set of rates had become unworkable.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains the parity, the intervention promise, the reserve requirement and the collective adjustment of the values. Describing only the peg leaves out the rest.
questions.hint: Name the parts a member had to provide.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a default on a foreign currency loan
questions.learningObjective: Read two simultaneous shocks behind a default
questions.stem: Projection note 352 asks how the sheet should read a default in which the borrower's currency fell at the same time as the export price.

options.text: Two shocks arrived together, so the burden on the debt rose and the income to meet it fell
The default was caused by the currency alone, since the price of exports did not move
options.misconception: ignores the fall in the export price

options.text: The default was caused by the export price alone, since the currency did not move
options.misconception: ignores the currency movement

options.text: The two movements were unrelated, since one concerned trade and the other finance
options.misconception: declares the two shocks unrelated

answer.exemplar: The road, port or power station was built for traffic that mostly began and ended abroad, so the people who would use it and pay for it were not the people whose tax receipts would have to cover the cost. questions.learningObjective: Explain what a borrower faced when the currency of its debt moved against it
questions.stem: Projection note 369 asks for a full written account of what a borrower faced when the currency of its debt moved against it.

answer.exemplar: The borrower owed a fixed amount of a foreign currency and earned its own, so a weaker currency turned a known bill into a larger one in the terms it actually paid in. Two things then happened at once: the debt service took a larger share of export earnings, and the country could not pay even the interest without drawing down reserves or borrowing more. A government facing that choice usually cut imports and spending, which slowed the economy and shrank the earnings base still further.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains the enlarged bill, the shrinking earnings and the resulting squeeze on the budget and the reserves. Describing only the accounting effect is incomplete.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a government gave up the sheltered home market for the world market
questions.stem: Sheet 112 asks for a full written account of why a government gave up the sheltered home market for the world market.

answer.exemplar: The home market had been protected by tariffs that made imported goods dear and by an exchange rate that made exports uncompetitive, so domestic firms had never had to meet a foreign price. When the state could no longer afford the subsidies and the protection, and when the currency had to be brought down to a level that foreign buyers would accept, the sheltered arrangement stopped working. Firms that had only ever sold at home had to learn to meet prices abroad, and that took time the country did not have.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a fixed rate system did to a country with a hostile payments position
questions.stem: Fold annotation 46 asks for a written account of what a fixed rate system did to a country whose payments position turned hostile.

answer.exemplar: A country with a persistent payments deficit kept drawing on its reserves at the fixed rate, because the rate did not move to correct the imbalance. Those reserves were the buffer that kept the promised rate credible, and they were being spent precisely when the country's exports were weakest. Once the reserves fell to the level where credibility could no longer be defended, the rate had to move, and it moved at the worst possible moment for exports already under pressure.

questions.explanation: A good answer shows reserves being drawn down to defend a rate, and the defence failing exactly when it was most needed. Describing only the devaluation misses it.

options.text: It was contested inside each country, because the gains were concentrated while the costs were spread

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the distribution of the bargain's gains to the domestic politics of the signatories, with concentrated winners and diffuse losers.
questions.hint: Show who gained and who paid inside each state.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Fixed exchange rates after the 1930s
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the fixed rate system eventually broke down
questions.stem: Fold annotation 54 asks the cartographer to choose the best description of why the fixed rate system eventually broke down.

options.text: The countries could no longer agree on how the adjustment should be shared, so the rates became untenable
The system worked as intended until the metal itself became scarce for every holder at once
options.misconception: invents a universal shortage of the metal

options.text: The countries abandoned the system because the trade rules made the rates unnecessary
options.misconception: claims trade rules made fixed rates redundant

options.text: The system collapsed because one country chose to leave, taking the whole arrangement with it
options.misconception: reduces the breakdown to the action of one country

questions.explanation: The system's weakness was that any needed adjustment had to be shared, and agreement on sharing proved impossible. One country's departure misplaces the cause.
questions.hint: Ask what the countries had to agree on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The reserve currency and the metal peg
questions.learningObjective: Read a reserve balance sheet to judge whether the peg was covered
questions.stem: Atlas entry 252 shows a table in which the foreign currency in the reserve bank exceeds the metal by two to one, and asks how the sheet should read the position.

options.text: The bank is comfortably covered, since foreign currency holdings usually exceed metal
options.misconception: treats a larger claim on metal as evidence of comfort

options.text: The bank could convert every holding at the published rate whenever asked
options.misconception: claims the gap does not limit conversion

options.text: The bank could not convert every holding at the published rate if all were presented
The bank no longer publishes a rate at all, since the metal backing had been given up
options.misconception: assumes the published rate was abandoned

questions.explanation: A foreign currency stock twice the size of the metal means the conversion promise exceeds the asset behind it by a wide margin. Reading that as comfort misjudges the table.
questions.hint: Compare the two lines before judging.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: From import substitution to export orientation
questions.learningObjective: Judge the link between export orientation and the opening of the world market
questions.stem: Sheet 126 says the sheet links the shift to export orientation with the arrival of the world market, and asks whether the link holds.

options.text: The link holds, because exports could only begin once the world market existed
options.misconception: treats the world market as the sole precondition

options.text: The link holds in one direction only, since the world market gave the sheltered strategy no protection
The link does not hold, because export orientation was chosen long before any world market
options.misconception: dates export orientation earlier than the evidence allows

options.text: The link holds in both directions, since the market and the strategy grew together
options.misconception: claims a mutual dependence the sequence denies

questions.explanation: A one-way link is the defensible reading: an open world market removed the protection the old strategy depended on. Both growing together overstates the sequence.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the link the evidence supports.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading the export composition of a growing region
questions.learningObjective: Explain the exposure implied by a chamber of commerce note

stimulus.body: Members supply 63 percent of what we sell abroad and about 9 percent of what we buy from abroad. When the foreign price of our staple falls, our members feel it at once; when the foreign price of what we import rises, they feel it just as sharply, and there is little else we can sell instead.

questions.stem: Legend entry 75 attaches a note from a chamber of commerce to the sheet and asks what it shows about exposure.

options.text: The note shows the region dependent on one staple for both what it sells and what it buys
options.misconception: reads the import side as a second export staple

options.text: The note shows the region with a strong two-way trade, so any price move is offset
options.misconception: assumes a two-way trade cancels the price exposure

options.text: The note shows the region able to switch suppliers quickly whenever a price moves
options.misconception: claims flexibility the note denies

options.text: The note shows the region exposed on one selling line and on its import bill at once

questions.explanation: The note describes exposure on both sides at once, a dominant selling line and a narrow range of imports. Reading the imports as a second export staple contradicts it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens on the import side.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a default on a foreign currency loan
questions.learningObjective: Read a default notice to diagnose the cause of the default
questions.stem: Projection note 420 asks for a written account of how a government should read the numbers in a default notice.

answer.exemplar: A default notice is a statement about a currency, not a verdict on a country. The figures to look for are what the borrower earns, in what currency, what it owes, in what currency, and what has happened to the rate between them. If the rate moved against the borrower, the same bill has become a larger one. The notice should also be read against the reserve position, since a borrower with reserves can bridge a bad year, while one without cannot.

questions.explanation: A good answer sets out the four elements to compare and what the reserve position adds. Treating a notice as a verdict on the government misses its diagnostic content.
questions.hint: List the four figures a reader should compare.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the first defaults revealed about lending
questions.learningObjective: Connect the first defaults to the standing of the countries that paid
questions.stem: Grid note 68 asks the cartographer to connect the first defaults to the standing of the countries that paid.

options.text: The defaults lowered the standing of the paying countries, because they had to repay what others failed to
options.misconception: reverses which group's standing was lowered

options.text: The defaults raised the standing of the paying countries, because their record of payment proved sound
options.misconception: claims the defaults improved the payers' reputation

options.text: The defaults raised the standing of the paying countries, and their credit became more attractive
The defaults left standing unchanged, because credit was assessed only on the borrower's file
options.misconception: denies that any group's standing shifted

questions.explanation: A synthesis must connect the experience of paying to the better terms those countries obtained, which raised their standing with lenders. Lowering their standing misreads the effect.
questions.hint: Show what the paying countries gained.
